summary: Wilhelm Gesenius was a linguistics and religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Helmstedt (~1803–1806) and the University of Göttingen (~1806). He held posts at Göttingen (~1806–1809) and the University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1810–1842).

Wilhelm Grube worked in Sinology and linguistics, studying at Saint Petersburg under Vasilyev and Schiefner, and at Leipzig under von der Gabelentz. He held posts at the Asiatic Museum, Ethnological Museum of Berlin, Leipzig University, and Humboldt University.
Wilhelm Gundert worked in Japanology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. Succeeding Karl Florenz, he held a post at the University of Hamburg from approximately 1936 to 1945.

Wilhelm Halbfass was an Indology and philosophy scholar who studied at Vienna and Göttingen. He held posts at the University of Göttingen (~1968–1971), the University of Pennsylvania (1982–2000), and as a visiting teacher at Hamburg (~1989–1990).

Wilhelm Havers was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He held academic posts at Leipzig University (~1913–1915), the University of Bern (~1915–1920), the University of Breslau (~1920–1928), the University of Würzburg (~1928–1937), and the University of Vienna (~1937–1953).

Wilhelm Max Müller was an archaeologist, historian, and linguist. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1883–1884) and Leipzig University (~1884–1888), and later held a post at the University of Pennsylvania (~1910–1919).

Wilhelm Pertsch studied under Albrecht Weber, Rudolf von Roth, and at Berlin and Tübingen. A scholar of Indology and Iranian and Central Asian studies, he held leadership posts at Forschungsbibliothek Gotha, Münzkabinett Gotha, and Wissenschaftliche Anstalten auf Schloss Friedenstein.
Wilhelm Printz was an Indology scholar who studied under Wilhelm Schulze (~1906–1910) and Heinrich Lüders (~1909–1911).

Wilhelm Rau studied Indology at Leipzig under Weller and Marburg under Nobel. He held professorships at Goethe University Frankfurt (1955) and Marburg (1958–1987, succeeding Nobel), and later taught at Leipzig (1992–1993).

Wilhelm Roscher studied at the University of Göttingen (~1835–1838) and Frederick William University Berlin (~1838–1840). He held posts at the University of Göttingen (~1840–1848), Leipzig University (~1848–1894), and Humboldt University of Berlin.

Wilhelm Scherer studied at Vienna and Berlin under Moriz Haupt and Franz Bopp. A linguist, he held posts at the University of Vienna (1864; 1868–1872), the University of Strasbourg (1872), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1877).

Wilhelm Schmidt, a scholar of linguistics and religious studies, studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1893–1895). He later held posts at the University of Vienna (~1906–1938) and the University of Fribourg (~1939–1951).

Wilhelm Schott was a scholar of Sinology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1823–1826) and later held a post there from approximately 1838 to 1889.

Wilhelm Schulze studied linguistics and Indology at Berlin under Schmidt, and at Greifswald under Zimmer, Kiessling, Kaibel, and Wilamowitz-Moellendorff. He held chairs at Marburg (1892), Göttingen (1895), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1902–1932), succeeding Schmidt.
Wilhelm Solf studied Indology under Richard Pischel at Halle-Wittenberg, and also studied at Berlin, Göttingen, Kiel, and Jena. He held a post at Kiel University.
Wilhelm Storck studied under Franz Bopp (~1851–1855) and Moriz Haupt (~1853–1855).

Wilhelm Streitberg studied linguistics and Indology at Münster, Leipzig (under Brugmann and Windisch), and Berlin. He held posts at Fribourg (~1889–1899), Münster (1899), Munich (1909–1920), and Leipzig (1898; 1920–1925, succeeding Brugmann).

Wilhelm Vatke, a scholar of religious studies and philosophy, studied at Halle-Wittenberg (~1824–1826), Berlin (~1826–1828), and Göttingen (~1828–1829). He held a post at Humboldt University of Berlin from approximately 1830 to 1882.

Wilhelm Wackernagel studied linguistics at Humboldt University of Berlin under Karl Lachmann and August Boeckh (1824–1827). He taught at Pädagogium Basel (~1833–1835) and held a professorship at the University of Basel (1833; 1835–1869).

Wilhelm Wundt, a scholar of philosophy, studied at Tübingen (~1851–1852), Heidelberg (~1852–1855), and Berlin (~1856). He held posts at the University of Zurich (1857), Leipzig University (1858), and Heidelberg University (1864).
